```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(dar)
set.seed(130)
```

`dar` provides a common interface for configuring, running and comparing
differential abundance methods. A recipe records preprocessing steps, a shared
statistical design and the methods to execute. The prepared recipe contains
per-method results; consensus is an optional summary, not a required endpoint.

## Example data

The included `metaHIV_phy` object is a `phyloseq` dataset from
[Noguera-Julian et al. (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2016.01.032).
Here we compare its recorded `RiskGroup2` categories. This unadjusted example
illustrates the software; it does not establish causal effects or validated
microbial biomarkers.

```{r data}
data("metaHIV_phy", package = "dar")
metaHIV_phy
```

## Configure a workflow

Create a recipe and define the model once with `add_model()`. `targets` selects
the variable whose effects are tested; other fixed terms can adjust for
covariates. `tax_level` selects the rank at which methods analyze the data.
An explicit reference makes the direction of comparisons clear.

```{r recipe}
rec <- recipe(metaHIV_phy) |>
  add_model(
    ~ RiskGroup2,
    targets = "RiskGroup2",
    tax_level = "Species",
    reference = c(RiskGroup2 = "hts")
  ) |>
  step_subset_taxa(tax_level = "Kingdom", taxa = c("Bacteria", "Archaea")) |>
  step_filter_by_prevalence(threshold = 0.03) |>
  step_deseq(id = "deseq") |>
  step_maaslin(min_prevalence = 0, id = "maaslin")

rec
```

The prevalence step retains taxa present in more than 3% of samples. We disable
MaAsLin3's additional prevalence filter because the recipe already defines a
shared filter; this does not make the engines' assumptions or effect scales
identical. These two compatible methods illustrate the interface, not a
universally recommended panel.

## Run the recipe

`prep()` applies preprocessing in order, resolves the shared model and runs
compatible methods. This guide uses sequential execution. For separate worker
processes, use `parallel = TRUE` and choose `workers` for the available memory.

```{r prepare}
fit <- prep(rec, parallel = FALSE)
fit
```

## Inspect per-method results

`tidy_results()` returns a common table with taxon IDs, contrasts, effect scales,
statistics and method decisions. `method` identifies the engine and `step_id`
identifies its configured instance. Native effect scales remain distinct;
uniform columns do not imply interchangeable effect sizes or p-values.

```{r results}
results <- tidy_results(fit)
results |>
  dplyr::select(
    taxa_id, contrast_id, effect_size, effect_metric,
    adj_p_value, significant, method, step_id
  ) |>
  head()

results |>
  dplyr::group_by(step_id, contrast_id) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_significant = sum(significant, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

These results can be used directly, without `bake()` or `cool()`.

## Plot a selected comparison

Plots accept explicit contrast selectors so distinct hypotheses are not mixed.
Here we show up to six taxa detected by at least one method for the comparison
of `msm` with `hts`. An empty selection is a valid result, not a plotting failure.

```{r abundance, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
comparison_id <- "RiskGroup2[msm-hts]"
taxa_ids <- results |>
  dplyr::filter(contrast_id == comparison_id, significant) |>
  dplyr::distinct(taxa_id) |>
  dplyr::pull(taxa_id) |>
  head(6)

if (length(taxa_ids)) {
  abundance_plt(
    fit, taxa_ids = taxa_ids,
    contrast_id = comparison_id, type = "boxplot"
  )
} else {
  message("No significant taxa for this comparison.")
}
```
